findings.title: D1's reasoning for re-entering the loop misreads how checkpoints work
findings.description:
The slice plan requires the design to "state and justify one answer" to the re-enterability question (`900-slices…md:192`). Two of D1's four reasons depend on a description of checkpoints that doesn't match the code:

- **Reason 2 (lines 161-166)** says a human who chose `Continue` at an in-loop checkpoint gets overridden by the current behavior. That can't happen. In `_execute_step_once`, `ACCEPT` and `OVERRIDE` (there is no "continue" option) inject instructions and carry on inside the step and the loop (`executor.py:1026-1028`). A step returns `PAUSED` only when the human picks `EXIT` (`executor.py:1018-1025`), or when the session is non-interactive and the prompt silently defaults to `EXIT` (`executor.py:338-343`). So the bug never touches a human who said "continue".
- **Reason 3 (lines 168-171)** says choosing `Exit` "ends the run" and stays available as the "human takes over" escape hatch, unaffected by re-entry. In fact `Exit` is the pause. It is the exact input this slice will turn into "resume re-enters the loop". Once the slice lands, a human who wants to take over from a paused loop has no way to say so; today that reading is the default.

The decision itself may still be right. In non-interactive runs, resuming is arguably the only "continue" signal there is. But the rationale has to be rewritten around the real triggers (`EXIT` and non-interactive default-exit). It should also state that "human takes over" will no longer be expressible, or else name how it can be expressed. The vocabulary also needs fixing: `checkpoint.py:106` offers `approve/revise/skip/abort`, while `CheckpointResolution` uses `accept/override/exit`. "Continue" appears in neither.

findings.title: Resuming at the paused round runs that round again, which contradicts "resume does not grant extra rounds"
findings.description:
The round number is recorded when the checkpoint fires. In the `[dispatch, review, checkpoint]` shapes the design lists (lines 105-112), that is after round N's dispatch and review have already finished. D3 then restarts at `range(start_iteration, …)` with `start_iteration = N`, so round N is dispatched and reviewed a second time. That is an extra round, against lines 181-182.

There is a worse case. A non-interactive run whose redo of round N again gets CONCERNS will default-exit and pause at N again. Every resume repeats round N and the loop never reaches `max:`. D1's own reason 2 says "proceed … means the next round" (line 165), which disagrees with the "resume at round N" rule. Pick one:
- Resume at N+1. Exhaustion is then handled when N = max.
- Or keep N, justify why the round is repeated, and explain how repeated pauses at the same round are bounded.

findings.title: Pauses from `on_exhaust: checkpoint` are not handled
findings.description:
`_loop_exhaust_result` also returns `PAUSED`, with `iteration=max_iter` (`executor.py:1064-1073`). This pause goes through the same `_append_step` path, so it is recorded the same way. Under Part A, resume now returns to the exhausted loop instead of moving past it. Under Part B, `resume_iteration_for` returns `max` and the loop runs round `max` again. That is an extra round, and it changes what `on_exhaust: checkpoint` means today ("all rounds used up, a human reviews, the run moves on"). D4's WARNING would also report "0 rounds not run" for a pause that didn't come from a short-circuit.

The design needs to tell exhaustion pauses apart from in-body checkpoint pauses and say what resume does with each. One option is to record the cause, or to have `resume_iteration_for` treat `iteration == max` as exhausted. Whichever is chosen needs a test.

findings.title: `resume_iteration_for` doesn't say which record it reads when there are several
findings.description:
`_append_step` always appends and never replaces (`state.py:304`). So a loop paused, resumed and paused again leaves several `StepState` entries with the same `step_name`. D2's set-based check handles that correctly. `resume_iteration_for` is only described as "return the recorded `iteration` for a named step", without saying it must take the latest entry. The design also doesn't cover three other cases:
- No entry exists for the step.
- The recorded iteration is greater than the current definition's `max` because the pipeline file was edited between pause and resume. `range(start, max+1)` would be empty and the loop would drop straight into the exhaustion branch without saying so.
- The entry is a `FAILED` step. Should that re-enter at its round, or restart?

Each of these needs a stated behavior and a test. Per the project's fail-fast rule, an out-of-range iteration should raise an error or at least log a WARNING, not quietly run zero rounds.

findings.title: The Part C WARNING leaves out the single-action loop, which has the same silent short-circuit
findings.description: `_execute_loop_step` stops on an inner `PAUSED` just as silently ("Checkpoint pause always stops the loop", `executor.py:1135-1137`). Part B threads `start_iteration` through both functions (line 289). The component table, however, adds the WARNING only to `_execute_loop_body`. The functional requirement at lines 305-306 says "a loop that short-circuits", which covers both. The table and the test list (line 318) should name both sites. Alternatively, move the log to the one place both return paths pass through.

findings.title: D2's prose and its code sketch describe different checks
findings.description: The prose says "present **and** in a terminal-complete status", which is an allow-list. The sketch excludes `{PAUSED, FAILED}`, which is a deny-list. With today's four `ExecutionStatus` members (`executor.py:132-135`) both give the same result, with `SKIPPED` counted as complete. They will diverge if a status is added later. Choose one and state it.
